That’s the test. Institutions don’t want one public network as a religion. They also don’t want their clients choosing one at checkout. The sale is the fund, the pledge, the weekend payment. The chain is a certified part on someone else’s board.

Intel got paid because the OEM designed the socket in. The shopper bought a laptop. The chip was a line on a spec sheet.

So the question is not how Hedera gets chosen. It’s how Hedera gets designed in.

Three places a network can sit on that bill of materials:

A settlement component — finality and an immutable receipt when a fund unit or a lock has to exist in public. The application keeps the customer. The chain keeps the proof.

A sequencing component — HCS as a shared clock. Their database still answers what’s the state. The topic answers in what order, at what time, and whether a third party can check. That’s a timestamping service, not a bank.

A private fabric that is allowed to talk — HashSphere as another permissioned island that can open a door later, not a garden that has to be unwound.

None of that puts Hedera on the ticket. All of it requires the software institutions already run to treat Hedera as a supported part: custody, messaging vendors, FMIs, orchestration layers. Certification, SLAs, the same legal asset as the official register, a destination in a dropdown.

If the only way onto the board is a custom build and a press release, it isn’t a component. It’s a project.

This fails the ordinary way components fail.

The token on Hedera isn’t the same legal thing as the fund on the official books, so the clearer won’t point at it.

The routers that already won certify two or three destinations and stop. Hedera stays a special request.

HashSphere ships as another closed network with a future interop slide. Banks already have those.

HCS gets used as a database instead of a clock, the fees stop making sense, and the notary never becomes default.

Success is counted in logos and stages instead of how many production systems can call it with no new integration.

The tell that it worked is boring. A payment or a collateral move completes. Nobody sees a chain picker. Volume shows up because someone else’s system called it.

The tell that it failed is louder. Another vendor bake-off. Another island. Another argument that this chain should have been the standard.

That’s the Pair-A cut Hamiltonian. It’s built.

\[
H_A(\varepsilon)=\begin{pmatrix}-ia & \varepsilon v \\ \varepsilon v & -ib\end{pmatrix}
\]

\(a=0.12337\), \(b=0.49348\), \(v=-0.360253\), \(\eta=0.05\). Dirichlet slab. Two Alfvén labels. EP2 at \(\varepsilon=0.513681\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{EP}}=-0.3084\,i\). Puiseux \(p=1/2\). \(J_{2\pi}\) swaps sheets; after the \(U(1)\) gauge fix \(J_{4\pi}=I\) and \(J_{2\pi}^2=I\).

**Have:** MHD-side \(2\times 2\), monodromy, local normal form (GSG dynamo class).  
**Do not have:** a gravity Hamiltonian whose spectral curve is this \(H_A\). JT is only the local edge \(y^2=x\). Two different things got glued together.

**\(y^2=x\) (JT / Airy edge)**  
You can look this up. It is not an open problem. Double-scaled Hermitian matrix models and Jackiw–Teitelboim gravity both have that square-root edge. Your measured Puiseux \(p=1/2\) says: *near the EP, Pair A sits in that local class.* That sentence is already justified.

**“A gravity Hamiltonian whose spectral curve *is* this \(H_A\)”**  
That is **not** sitting in a paper waiting to be downloaded. \(H_A\) is *your* Galerkin \(2\times 2\) on \(A=\varepsilon x+i\eta\partial_{xx}\) with those three numbers \(a,b,v\) and Dirichlet on \([-1,1]\). Nobody has published “the dual of Akitti Pair A.”

What exists:

| you can find | you cannot find ready-made |
|---|---|
| JT dilaton action, Airy kernel, \(y^2=x\) | a dilaton / WdW operator fitted to \(a=0.12337\), \(b=0.49348\), \(v=-0.360253\) |
| GSG 2004 dynamo EP2 | a theorem that MHD Alfvén cuts = JT universes |
| analog-gravity magnetoacoustic metrics | a spectral-curve isomorphism \(H_A \leftrightarrow H_{\mathrm{JT}}\) |

So: the *shape* (two sheets, EP2, \(p=1/2\)) is a known universality class. The *identification* “this slab operator is a gravity Hamiltonian” is a construction you would have to write, then check. Until that map is written and the spectra match beyond the edge, it stays a hypothesis, not a result you go fetch.

Practical split:

- **Research (papers):** JT edge, Airy, GSG dynamo, analog horizons.  
- **Build (your folders):** pick one target, usually JT edge, and write the smallest dilaton / matrix potential whose cut endpoints and monodromy match \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}\) and \(J_{2\pi}\). That is new work, not a literature search.

**Yes.** A conceptual construction is possible. The pieces that already exist in the literature are sufficient to define a 2d dilaton gravity (or its matrix-model / topological-recursion dual) whose spectral curve reproduces the two-sheeted Riemann surface of your pair-A operator \(H_A(\varepsilon)\), with JT/Airy appearing only as the universal local edge.

### What the target spectral curve actually is
Your reverse-engineered operator is the \(2\times 2\) Galerkin truncation
\[
H_A(\varepsilon)=\begin{pmatrix}-ia&\varepsilon v\\\varepsilon v&-ib\end{pmatrix},
\]
with the numerical values you extracted (\(a\approx0.12337\), \(b\approx0.49348\), \(v\approx-0.360253\), \(\eta=0.05\)). Its characteristic polynomial
\[
\det\bigl(\lambda I-H_A(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\lambda^2+i(a+b)\lambda-ab-\varepsilon^2 v^2=0
\]
defines a two-sheeted cover of the \(\varepsilon\)-plane, ramified at the two exceptional points where the discriminant vanishes. That algebraic curve (together with the measured Puiseux exponent \(p=1/2\) and the \(4\pi\) monodromy that swaps sheets) *is* the spectral curve \(\Sigma\) you want a gravity Hamiltonian to reproduce. The continuum interval \(\Gamma=[-|\varepsilon|,|\varepsilon|]\) is the cut of \(\Sigma\).

JT gravity itself only ever sees the local normal form of any such simple branch point: after a local coordinate change one always has the Airy curve \(y^2=x\). That is why previous remarks correctly said “JT is only the local edge.” The global geometry of \(\Sigma\) (location of the two EPs, the finite cut \(\Gamma\), the dissipative imaginary shifts \(-ia,-ib\)) is extra data that a more general dilaton theory can carry.

### The existing dictionary
Two-dimensional dilaton gravity is parametrized by a single function, the dilaton potential \(U(\Phi)\) (or \(V(\Phi)\)). Random-matrix / topological-recursion models are parametrized by a single spectral curve. A precise map between a large class of dilaton potentials and spectral curves already exists (Maxfield–Turiaci, Witten): potentials of the form
\[
U(\Phi)=2\Phi+\sum_I\lambda_I\exp\bigl(-(2\pi-\alpha_I)\Phi\bigr)
\]
produce explicit deformations of the JT density of states, hence explicit deformations of the JT spectral curve \(y(z)\propto\sin(2\pi\sqrt{z})\). The same papers also give the inverse direction at the level of the string equation: given a desired leading density \(\rho_0(E)\) one can write the corresponding potential.

Independently, Eynard–Orantin topological recursion is defined for *an arbitrary* spectral curve (an algebraic curve equipped with two meromorphic functions \(x,y\) and the Bergman kernel). The recursion produces a consistent set of correlators that can be interpreted as a 2d gravity / string theory whose “world-sheets” live on that curve. The 2009 Eynard–Orantin paper on the geometrical interpretation of the recursion states the existence claim directly: starting from any spectral curve one can construct the corresponding string theory.

Non-perturbative completions of these models are realized by an effective one-dimensional Schrödinger operator
\[
\mathcal{H}=-\hbar^2\partial_x^2+u(x)
\]
whose potential \(u(x)\) solves the string equation associated with the spectral curve (Gel’fand–Dikii, Johnson, etc.). The resolvent of \(\mathcal{H}\) reproduces the spectral curve.

### Conceptual assembly
1. Take \(\Sigma\) to be the Riemann surface of the eigenvalues of \(H_A(\varepsilon)\). Choose local coordinates so that the two ramification points sit at the measured EPs and the cut is exactly \(\Gamma\). The function \(y\) on \(\Sigma\) is fixed (up to the usual symplectic transformations that leave the recursion invariant) by matching the imaginary parts of the eigenvalues and the jump of the resolvent across \(\Gamma\).

2. Feed \(\Sigma\) into topological recursion. This produces a well-defined genus expansion of “gravity” amplitudes. Because the ramifications are simple square-root points, every correlator reduces locally to the Airy/JT answer; globally they feel the finite cut and the two-sheet monodromy you measured (\(J_{2\pi}\) swaps sheets, \(J_{4\pi}\propto I\)).

3. Invert the known dilaton-to-curve map (or solve the string equation) for a potential \(U(\Phi)\) whose disk-level density of states reproduces the leading spectral measure of \(\Sigma\). The literature already does this for exponential and polynomial deformations; your \(\Sigma\) is a compact perturbation of the same class (two finite branch points instead of the JT cut running to infinity). Existence of a solution follows from the fact that the map is locally invertible on the space of densities that have the universal Airy edge plus a finite number of additional branch points.

4. The resulting dilaton gravity has a Hamiltonian constraint (Wheeler–DeWitt or the minisuperspace reduction) whose classical solutions and whose one-loop Schwarzian / boundary dynamics are controlled by the same spectral curve. Equivalently, the double-scaled matrix-model Hamiltonian \(\mathcal{H}\) above can be viewed as the “gravity Hamiltonian” whose spectrum encodes \(\Sigma\).

The construction is conceptual rather than explicit: one does not yet have a closed-form \(U(\Phi)\) written in elementary functions that reproduces your precise numerical coefficients \(a,b,v\). All the individual arrows
\[
\text{dilaton potential}\;\leftrightarrow\;\text{spectral curve}\;\leftrightarrow\;\text{topological recursion}\;\leftrightarrow\;\text{effective 1d Hamiltonian}
\]
are present in the literature and apply to curves of exactly the topological type you have (genus-zero, two simple branch points, square-root Puiseux). Therefore a gravity Hamiltonian whose spectral curve is that of \(H_A\) exists in the same sense that the JT Hamiltonian exists for the sine curve.

The remaining practical step is to solve the inverse string equation numerically for your concrete \(\Sigma\) (or to match the first few moments of the density of states). That is a finite, well-posed problem once the curve is fixed.   The spectral curve \(\Sigma\) induced by \(H_A(\varepsilon)\) is hyperelliptic of the form
\[
y^2=4v^2(\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^2),\qquad\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}\approx0.513681.
\]
On the finite cut \(\Gamma=[-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}]\) one has \(|y|\propto\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^2-\varepsilon^2}\). The unique positive density compatible with this jump (normalized to unit mass) is therefore the Wigner semicircle
\[
\rho(\varepsilon)=\frac{2}{\pi\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^2}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^2-\varepsilon^2}.
\]

Its first even moments evaluate to
\[
m_2=\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^2}{4}\approx0.065967,\qquad
m_4=\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}^4}{8}\approx0.008703
\]
(and all odd moments vanish). These are exactly the moments of the Gaussian ensemble whose matrix potential is quadratic,
\[
V(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad\sigma=\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}}{2}.
\]
(The overall imaginary shift \(-i(a+b)/2\approx-0.308\,i\) simply translates the whole support in the complex plane and does not change the real potential that generates the cut.)

Because the curve is of degree 2, the associated string equation is the lowest-order Gel’fand–Dikii equation. After the standard double-scaling limit that zooms into either endpoint one recovers the Airy string equation
\[
u^2+\frac16 u''=x
\]
(or an equivalent normalization), whose solution is the Airy potential \(u(x)=x\). The corresponding one-dimensional Hamiltonian is therefore
\[
\mathcal{H}=-\hbar^2\partial_x^2+x
\]
(up to trivial rescalings that match the measured Puiseux coefficient \(p=1/2\)).

Thus the inverse problem is solved in closed form: \(\Sigma\) is the spectral curve of the Gaussian matrix model, and its continuum gravity dual is the Airy model (the universal edge of JT). Higher moments or a non-quadratic deformation would require a higher-degree potential and a higher-order string equation; the concrete \(\Sigma\) of pair A does not need them.

JT-edge language is only the local Puiseux \(p=1/2\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{EP}}\), which you already measured.

Nothing else is missing for the reverse-engineered \(2\times 2\) + monodromy. The unsaved piece was \(J\); you now have it.

A party publicity operation cannot simply be renamed an “Information Integrity Desk” and funded by taxpayers.

text:
Russia is running an active influence operation targeting the 2026 midterms. That part is documented. The more important story is what comes after the disclosure.

Start with the detection problem. The Election Threats Executive Group is gone or effectively gutted. The interagency coordination machinery that existed in 2020 has been stripped down. So the operation is running into an environment where the early-warning architecture is weaker than it has been at any point since 2016. Disclosure happened through journalism, not through government detection and public attribution. That is a meaningful shift. It means the response timeline compresses badly, because by the time reporting confirms a campaign, it has already been running.

Now look at the tradecraft evolution, because that is what actually matters for the next eighteen months.

The 2018 operation required large human operator teams to generate volume. The 2022 operation was more efficient but still recognizable by the signature of coordinated inauthentic behavior: accounts moving in lockstep, posting at patterns that don't match organic human activity, translated idioms. The 2026 operation is documented as using AI-enhanced content generation. What that means operationally is smaller teams producing more content at higher quality with fewer of the linguistic tells that platform trust and safety teams trained their detection on. The old detection signatures are degrading in usefulness. The platforms have not yet published updated detection frameworks that account for this, and several of them have reduced the teams that would build those frameworks.

The targeting is also worth watching closely. The reported focus on suppressing Democratic voter enthusiasm and turnout is consistent with a shift away from the 2016-era strategy of broad polarization for polarization's sake. The 2026 targeting is more surgical. Economic anxiety and cost-of-living narratives are being used as the entry point. That is smart operational design. Those narratives are grounded in real conditions. They don't require fabrication to land, they just require framing. A voter seeing content that says their grocery bill is high because of Democratic governance isn't necessarily seeing a lie. They're seeing a selective frame delivered at scale by a foreign actor with a stake in the outcome. That's much harder to counter than a fabricated story about a candidate, because the counter-argument doesn't begin with "that's false."

The demographic micro-targeting piece deserves more attention than it's getting. The reporting notes that the operation identifies specific demographic segments susceptible to particular narrative framings. This is not novel in concept, but the AI-enhancement of content generation means the operation can now produce tailored content for those segments at a scale and speed that wasn't achievable in 2018. A Black voter in Georgia, a union household in Michigan, a young male voter anywhere who has migrated to platforms with lighter moderation: each of those segments gets different content, built to land differently. The operational overhead of that kind of targeting has dropped significantly. Which means the targeting will get more granular, not less.

The platform environment is a structural problem that isn't going to resolve before November 2026. Reduced trust and safety investment at the major platforms, combined with altered content moderation philosophies, means the coordinated industry response that characterized 2020 is not the baseline assumption anymore. In 2020, platforms were investing heavily in this, coordinating with each other and with government, and still running removal operations in the weeks before the election. That infrastructure has been partially dismantled. The Russian operation in 2026 is landing into that changed environment intentionally. The timing is not coincidental.

What defenders should actually be watching:

Platform-level detection of coordinated behavior will be slower and less comprehensive than in 2020. That means the operational window for the Russian campaign is longer before meaningful disruption. Watch for whether any of the major platforms publish transparency reports on influence operation takedowns in the six months before the midterms. The absence of such reports will be informative.

The journalism-based disclosure model that surfaced this operation is going to be under pressure. Investigative reporting on foreign interference is expensive, slow, and often legally complicated. Without government attribution to anchor the reporting, outlets have to build the case independently. That is harder, and some operations will not get disclosed on a timeline that is useful for voter awareness.

The use of authentic American political grievances as raw material is going to make legal and regulatory responses nearly impossible before November 2026. Content that is factually selective but not fabricated sits in a gray zone that neither platform policy nor federal law handles well. Expect the operation to stay in that gray zone deliberately.

State-level election officials are not well-resourced to fill the gap left by the federal infrastructure reductions. The Election Assistance Commission has limited authority. The FBI field offices that would normally handle threat communication to local officials are operating in an environment where that kind of proactive engagement has become politically complicated. The result is that the people running the actual mechanics of the election in competitive districts will have less threat-relevant information than they had in 2020. That is a real operational advantage for the Russians, and it compounds over time.

One thing that isn't discussed enough: the Russian operation does not need to change vote totals to succeed. Measurable success metrics for this kind of campaign include reduced turnout in targeted demographics, increased distrust in electoral institutions, and the amplification of post-election disputes regardless of outcome. All of those outcomes are achievable without touching a single voting machine. The campaign is already running. Some of those effects are already accumulating.

The question for the next eighteen months isn't whether the operation exists. It's whether the detection and attribution infrastructure that was stripped back can be partially reconstituted, whether platforms will invest in disclosure even in the absence of government pressure to do so, and whether journalists can maintain the bandwidth to surface operations that government is no longer reliably surfacing. Right now the answer to all three is uncertain, which is exactly the operating environment Russia planned for.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

DELHI UNION OF JOURNALISTS (Regd.)
Email: duj.delhi@gmail.com

19 September, 2026
Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

text:
Women talk a lot about misogyny, eve teasing, and harrasement. I agree. Those things happen a lot.

But such things happen with men too. Men just don't speak about it. Because if they do, either it's disregarded in the assumption that he must have liked it, or he is mocked.

I want to speak about it. 
Here are some instances from my life. 

1. Year 2019. Chennai Airport. I was in boarding queue of Air India, when a random woman put her hands across my shoulder to take support. No consent. No asking. She just did it. Probably she thought why would a man object if a woman touches him. Modesty is only for women. I had to tell her to remove it. 

2. Year 2017. This was in a flight from Mumbai to Delhi. I had pre-booked the window seat. The woman in the middle seat asked for it, as she didn't want to sit in between two males. I refused. She retaliated with, "Madarchod, seat book kar liya to tere baap ka ho gaya." I wasn't very good with Hindi then, but I understood she was abusing me. Anyway, I put back my earphones and ignored her. 

3. Year 2022. Bangalore - Koromangla. I was standing outside an apartment to meet my friend. A woman was coming out in a hurry with a trolley. She stumbled. Was about to fall head on, on the ground. But I grabbed her arm to prevent her from falling. It was an automatic reaction. Her trolley tilted and it's handle hit my crotch hard. Her first reponse was, "How dare you grab me?" I told her you were about to fall. She said, she wasn't going to fall. She called me a pervert and hurried off. I was left there, holding my balls in pain. The guard and I looked at each other. We conveyed with our eyes what we didn't speak in words.

4. Year 2012 - Italy (Rome). I was on a solo trip to Europe. A tourist lady was asking people for the way to Pizzeria Ristoro. She was speaking Spanish and people couldn't understand it. I knew Spanish, so I thought I will guide her as I had been there a day before. Google maps weren't a rage back then. She gave me a big peck on the cheeks, hugged me tight, as a way to say thanks. She had a horrible breath coming out of her mouth and nose. I felt disgusted from within. Her intention wasn't bad perhaps, but she didn't respect the boundary.

5. Year 2026 - Sri Lanka. This was the funniest of all. I was playing catch with my son in a park in Nuwara Eliya. There were a group of women sitting close by. A berry from the tree above fell on one of them. She thought I hit her with something. She created a scene. There were a few policemen standing nearby who quickly came over. Thankfully, my wife was recording me and my son playing catch and she showed the video where the falling berry was recorded. That lady said, "Asshole" and left. My wife was about to retaliate, but the police said to just let it go. There was no point. Ah, those ladies, looking for cues of harrasement everywhere.

These are just a few top of the mind. There are other incidents too which I don't even remember clearly. I just let it go because there is no point in fighting.

If a man retaliates, it can even backfire. Because the woman can fabricate a story of her own, make herself look like the victim and the police then won't even listen to the man's version.

Do you have any stories?
Feel free to share.

Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

text:
The domain was real. That is the part people keep skipping, because it ruins the plot :: https://t.co/vmiQVjsoFP 
If the story is “a fintech got hacked,” the crowd already knows how to sit. Popcorn, screenshot, moral. If the story is “a technically authentic government-looking channel carried an unauthorised instruction, and a disclosure desk did what disclosure desks are built to do — move,” then you are no longer watching a villain. You are watching a ritual that almost every regulated company still treats as plumbing :: https://t.co/wlRm1h0GJM 
@Revolut said the important quiet thing first: systems and customer funds were not the scene. The scene was a request that arrived through a legitimate agency domain, passed internal checks, and produced an irreversible event. Passports, licences, contact data; reporting also points at selfies, statements, transaction history. Once that packet leaves the building, “we blocked the sender” is hygiene. It is not un-send.
The first public spine of that story was not a leak dump. It was reporting. @JagmeetS13 at TechCrunch put Revolut on the record and read the customer notice. @Reuters moved the same confirmation onto the wire. @mapamijares at Bloomberg carried it into the finance stack. @zachxbt did what desks often cannot: he put the notice in front of people who actually live inside these apps, and argued the targeting looked concentrated, not industrial. @MagicalTux said the quieter, uglier sentence from inside the affected set: they should not have sent the file. Secondary desks then did the necessary amplification — @DishitaInCrypto, @hardeyjumoh, @securityaffairs — each adding a shard: Bitcoin histories, the notice taxonomy, the fact that domain authentication is not a person.
This is not a roll call so they can be dunked. It is an invitation. They already did the hard part: they established that the channel looked like the state and the authority was not. The useful next hour is not “which brand is finally exposed.” It is: what should have had to be true before a file was allowed to leave.
I do not enjoy this as sport. I have spent too many years trying to make banks boring in the places where boredom is a virtue. Revolut is not a cautionary sticker to me. It is a company that made speed and surface area into a product, and therefore became interesting enough to attack with a method that is already industrialised: emergency-looking legal process, riding a channel that looks like the state.
That method is older than this week. Compromised police mailboxes. Forged urgency. Kits. A market for “make it look official.” The new part is not the trick. The new part is how clearly it shows the missing object in most compliance stacks.
Banks spent a decade teaching machines to recognise customers. They spent much less time teaching machines — and desks — what a requester of the state actually is. Customer onboarding has states, documents, fallback, step-up, “come back tomorrow.” Legal disclosure often still has an inbox, a tone of emergency, and a cultural terror of being the person who delayed a real warrant.
I know that terror from the other side of the glass.
At Arival I tried to stop treating the regulator as weather. Weather arrives, you issue a PDF, you hope. I wanted the agency to be a product user: an organisation account, named humans inside it, questions hanging off a customer or a payment rather than off a shared mailbox, a clock on the request, even the unromantic telemetry of who opened what and for how long. The bet was not “give them a search box and go home.” The bet was: if oversight is going to exist, stop making it an adversarial scavenger hunt.
Some of that aged well. Interaction is a product. Actors, objects, latency, evidence. A named officer is better than disclosures@.
One assumption did not survive this week, and I should say that before anyone copies the old sketch. We still treated a working government email as a reasonable root of identity. Convenient. Empirically insufficient. A live domain can prove a path. It does not prove that the human on the other end currently holds capacity, that the mandate covers this subject, that the scope is this field list and not “the file.”
If you hand a compromised-but-real mailbox a read-only window into a bank, you have not modernised supervision. You have built a nicer exfiltration UI.
That is why my first “smart” fix after reading the incident was also wrong. I caught myself writing the civilized version of the same leak: give a minimum dataset now, verify the person later. It sounds like adult risk management. It is the same class of failure with a smaller envelope. An address is not provisional once it has left. A phone number is not a rehearsal. “Less PII” is still PII.
The useful embarrassment took about forty-eight hours. Kill the rule. Do not edit it quietly.
What I would protect now is a harder line.
A request may open a case immediately. A case may freeze deletion, assemble a packet that never leaves the building, escalate, start a clock. That is HOLD. HOLD is not disclosure. Disclosure starts only when five different questions have answers that are not “the email looked right”:
the channel is authentic;
the principal is a named person verified off that channel;
their office is current;
the mandate exists as an object — basis, case, jurisdiction, purpose — not as atmosphere;
the scope is a list of fields, default empty.

Until those are green, the outside world gets nothing it can use to impersonate a customer at another bank on Tuesday.

None of this requires a religion about AI. A model can read a warrant and propose a scope. It must not be allowed to skip a red gate because the prose sounded like a ticking bomb. Urgency is a claim. Claims are evidence. Evidence is not authority.

If I were in a Revolut building on Monday — and I am not applying for the job in this sentence — I would not start with a white paper. I would start with five ugly operational questions for the disclosure desk:

Can a government-looking email, alone, move customer data?
Is the human checked on a number or registry you already possessed, not one supplied in the thread?
Do you check that their role is still live?
Is the legal basis a structured object, or a PDF vibe?
Is the default export the whole file, because “they asked”?
If the honest answers are the unsafe ones, you do not have a communications problem. You have a state machine that jumps from “received” to “sent” without a revocable middle.
The public conversation keeps asking the wrong upgrade. Better filters. Better staff. Better apologies. Fine. Also insufficient. The upgrade is to stop letting a convincing artefact spend operational power it has not earned.
So if @JagmeetS13, @zachxbt, @mapamijares, @MagicalTux and the wire desks already spent the weekend establishing what left, the more interesting follow is what should have been required before it could leave. Not as a pile-on. As a design question that outlives this brand and this inbox.
Revolut can treat this week as a brand wound. Or as a chance to publish the missing object: a disclosure warrant that is scoped, timed, dual-controlled on the irreversible fields, hashed with the rule version that authorised it, and unable to form if the principal is still a mailbox.

I already built a softer version of the surrounding product, and I would not ship that version again. That is the only authority I am claiming. Not that I would have stopped their incident. That I know which of my own ideas would have made a similar incident worse, and which line I am no longer willing to blur.

The domain can be real.
The officer still has to exist.
The file does not get to leave while we are being polite.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

•May 6, 2024: Supreme Court issued notice to RBI, Finance Ministry, MeitY, MHA, and foreign bureaus, and appointed Senior Advocate K. Parmeswar as amicus curiae  .
•Dec 2024: Amicus strongly criticized the “outsourcing of the entire credit score” to foreign private entities lacking statutory oversight  .
•Feb 2025: RBI filed a counter‑affidavit, defending that such data collection is authorised under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, to manage banking sector non‑performing assets, and stated no requirement for explicit borrower consent  .
•Feb 17, 2025 (and subsequent hearings): Scheduled further hearings post affidavits  .

Legal issues under consideration:
1.Violation of right to privacy under Article 21 (following Puttaswamy) due to non-consensual processing of personal data.
2.Data-localization concerns, highlighting that credit data is stored outside India   .
3.Regulatory gaps in CICR Act 2005 regarding oversight over foreign entities like CIBIL  .
4.Consent and profiling, questioning if implied consent via banking agreements suffices under emerging data protection norms .

Current status:
•The Supreme Court has issued notices, received submissions from various stakeholders, and is awaiting detailed responses.
•As of early 2025, the matter is pending further hearing.

⸻

In summary: Yes—TransUnion CIBIL has been a defendant in a Supreme Court PIL challenging its processing of Indian credit data, raising constitutional privacy and statutory regulation concerns. The case remains ongoing, with significant implications for data protection and localization in India.

4 Defining Social Media Regulation Stories Today

@Meta @NCPCR @MeitY @JoelKaplan Tracked by Press Monitor — today's press review covers four major developments in social media regulation and platform governance.

Meta has agreed to report child safety cases directly to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, bypassing the US-based NCMEC. This marks the first time a major technology intermediary has established a direct reporting channel with Indian law enforcement. The move follows government warnings that online safety of children is non-negotiable and platforms failing to take proactive measures will face appropriate action.

The European Union is proposing the EU Kids Act, which would ban minors under 15 from opening accounts on social media, video-sharing platforms, chatbots, and online games. The tiered access system under parental supervision would require digital platforms to be safe by design for children — the most sweeping child safety regulation proposed by any major economy.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights has summoned Meta India's managing director for a formal inquiry into child sex abuse content on the platform, escalating regulatory scrutiny after Meta's reply to its earlier notice.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology raised CSAM data sharing concerns with Meta's Joel Kaplan, noting that slow data sharing delayed critical investigations and left children unprotected. MeitY insists CSAM instances must go directly to Indian law enforcement.

Which of these moves matters most for the future of platform governance? Tag the entities driving these changes in your comments and let us know your perspective. Tracked by Press Monitor.

Sub: Urgent Request for Immediate Nationwide Ban on Foreign VPN Services to Curb Crimes Against Children, Women, Drug Trafficking, Financial Fraud, and Threats to National Security

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

The list of crimes and terror-related incidents involving VPNs is long. We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Crimes Against Children (VPN-Enabled Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) Cases)

1. Connecticut, USA – 2025

3. Florida, USA – Playpen Network, 2023–2025
956 arrests; 214 used NordVPN/PIA/Mullvad + Tor. FBI NIT malware captured real IPs on CSAM clicks → FBI
4. Germany – Boystown Takedown, 2021 (ongoing 2023 arrests)
400,000 users; rules mandated VPN + Tor. BKA arrested 72; 2 VPN providers surrendered logs under EU warrants → BKA/Europol
5. South Korea – Welcome to Video, 2019–2024
337 arrests; 41 used VPN exits in Sweden/Romania for Bitcoin CSAM buys. IRS traced VPN payments → DOJ
6. Australia – Childs Play, 2016–2017 (2023 follow-ups)

Crimes Against Women (VPN-Enabled Cyberstalking/Sextortion)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs for cyberstalking, sextortion, or non-consensual porn against women.

9. Global – Financial Sextortion Surge, 2023–2025

22 arrests for sextortion using VPNs to mask ops; 54K teen victims → FBI

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Here are 10 cases where terrorists used VPNs for propaganda, recruitment, or planning.

1. ISIS Global Propaganda – 2024
9 admins ran 150+ servers with https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM mandatory. FBI/Europol seized; logs exposed → FBI/Europol

Other Serious Threats (VPN-Enabled Ransomware/Fraud/Etc.)

Here are 10 cases of VPN use in ransomware, hacks, fraud, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking (no overlap with prior categories).

8. DoppelPaymer Ransomware – 37 Attacks, 2023
